title_en: Supreme People's Court Releases Typical Maritime Trial Cases
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court Releases Typical Cases of Maritime Trial

Case 1

China Wei Shipping Company, Chen Zhen, Chen Chun v. Mitsui O.S.K. Lines, Ltd. — dispute over time charterparty and tort damages

I. Basic Facts

China Wei Shipping Company (hereinafter referred to as China Wei) was established in Shanghai by Chen Shuntong in the early 1930s and ceased operations around 1940. The vessels "Shun Feng" and "Xin Tai Ping" (hereinafter collectively referred to as the Two Vessels) were owned by Chen Shuntong. The Two Vessels were operated by China Wei, and their port of registry was Shanghai. The company had no other investors.

On June 16, 1936 and October 14, 1936, Chen Shuntong, on behalf of China Wei, entered into two time charterparties in Shanghai with Daido Kaiun Kaisha, Ltd. (the predecessor of Mitsui O.S.K. Lines, Ltd.) for the Two Vessels, each for a period of twelve calendar months. The contracts stipulated the method of payment of hire, the place of redelivery, and other terms. The exception clause in the contracts provided that the vessels should not be required to call at any port that was in a state of blockade or where hostilities were taking place, nor carry contraband, nor undertake any voyage that might involve a risk of seizure, detention, or penalty by any ruler or government, nor carry such cargo. After the contracts were signed, the Two Vessels were delivered to Daido Kaiun Kaisha, Ltd. at the port of Shanghai. In August 1937, the Two Vessels were detained by the Japanese military at Osaka and Yawata, Japan. Subsequently, the Japanese Ministry of Communications entrusted the Two Vessels to Daido Kaiun Kaisha, Ltd. for operation in the form of a time charterparty. In 1938 and 1944, the Two Vessels were respectively wrecked by striking a reef and sunk.

On August 8, 1949, Chen Shuntong made a will, bequeathing all rights and interests in the Two Vessels and the unpaid hire therefor to his son Chen Qiaqun. On December 31, 1987, Chen Qiaqun made a will, authorizing his sons Chen Zhen and Chen Chun to act as his agents in litigation against Japan. China Wei, Chen Zhen, and Chen Chun filed a lawsuit with the Shanghai Maritime Court against Mitsui O.S.K. Lines, Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Mitsui O.S.K.), claiming hire for the Two Vessels, loss of operating income, and loss of the vessels, totaling JPY 2,916,477,260.80.

II. Judgment

The Shanghai Maritime Court held after trial that the plaintiff bringing the lawsuit was China Wei, which was established by Chen Qiaqun. This company was neither a party to the time charterparties in question nor the registered owner of the Two Vessels, and thus had no right to claim rights under the time charterparties or rights as the property owner. The Two Vessels were the personal property of Chen Shuntong. Chen Zhen and Chen Chun, by virtue of the wills, had legal basis to exercise the right to claim compensation for the Two Vessels.

Payment of hire was the charterer's contractual obligation. Mitsui O.S.K. should pay the outstanding hire to the shipowner. The fact that the Two Vessels were not directed to sail in safe waters, resulting in their detention by the Japanese military, was a consequence of Daido Kaiun Kaisha, Ltd.'s breach of contract. According to the Maritime Code of the PRC, the shipowner was entitled to rescind the contract and claim compensation for losses suffered thereby. Daido Kaiun Kaisha, Ltd., knowing that the owner of the vessels was Chen Shuntong, continued to retain possession of the Two Vessels without promptly informing the owner of the details or paying the contractual fees, which constituted a tort against the property rights holders of the Two Vessels. Given that the Two Vessels had been lost, Daido Kaiun Kaisha, Ltd. should bear tort liability for compensation for the actual economic losses incurred by the shipowner.

Where a civil right was infringed for more than twenty years before the implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC, the limitation period for the right holder to seek protection from a people's court after the implementation of that Law shall be calculated from January 1, 1987. In accordance with the law, the limitation period for the claims for payment of hire under the time charterparties and the tort claims was two years. Both claims had a limitation period expiring on December 31, 1988. The lawsuit filed by China Wei on December 30, 1988 was within the limitation period. The limitation period in this case was interrupted by the filing of the lawsuit by China Wei, and there was no issue of limitation period for Chen Zhen and Chen Chun joining the proceedings.

On December 7, 2007, the Shanghai Maritime Court rendered civil judgment (1989) Hu Hai Fa Shang Zi No. 25: dismissing the claims of China Wei; ordering Mitsui O.S.K. to pay and compensate Chen Zhen and Chen Chun for the hire, operating losses, vessel losses, and interest on the Two Vessels, totaling JPY 2,916,477,260.80.

China Wei, Chen Zhen, Chen Chun, and Mitsui O.S.K. all appealed the first-instance judgment to the Shanghai High People's Court. On August 6, 2010, the High Court rendered final judgment (2008) Hu Gao Min Si (Hai) Zhong Zi No. 80, dismissing the appeals of all parties. Mitsui O.S.K. applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. On December 23, 2010, the Supreme People's Court issued civil ruling (2010) Min Shen Zi No. 1269, dismissing the application for retrial.

Since Mitsui O.S.K. failed to perform the obligations determined in the effective judgment, the Shanghai Maritime Court, on April 19, 2014, lawfully arrested the 226,434-ton vessel "BAOSTEEL EMOTION," owned by Mitsui O.S.K., which had arrived at Majishan Port, Shengsi, Zhoushan, Zhejiang Province, China. On April 23, 2014, Mitsui O.S.K., in compliance with the Shanghai Maritime Court's Notice of Time Limit for Performance, fully performed all obligations determined in the effective judgment. On April 24, 2014, the Shanghai Maritime Court ordered the release of the "BAOSTEEL EMOTION" and issued an Order for Release of Arrested Vessel.

III. Significance

This case concerns a dispute over a time charterparty and tort damages. The performance of the charterparty and the loss of the subject matter occurred in the 1930s and 1940s, a long time ago. The court's trial focused on the rights and obligations agreed between the parties in the contract, whether the parties had breached the contract, and the corresponding liability for breach. This case is an ordinary commercial contract and tort damages dispute.

There are three key points in this case: First, determination of the facts and the nature of the case. Due to the long-standing nature of the dispute, both parties submitted extensive evidence to support their claims. The court held multiple hearings and examined all evidence item by item, ensuring that the determination of facts was fully supported by evidence. Regarding the characterization of the case, Daido Kaiun Kaisha, Ltd. failed to pay hire as agreed under the contract and did not arrange for the Two Vessels to sail in safe waters; instead, it arranged for the Chinese-flagged vessels to sail along the coast of Japan, leading to their detention by the Japanese military. Daido Kaiun Kaisha, Ltd. not only breached the contract, but also its breach had a legal causal relationship with the damage and loss of the Two Vessels, constituting a tort against the property rights holders of the Two Vessels. Second, the issue of the parties' standing. The plaintiffs, through inheritance by will and other means, three generations of the family (grandfather, father, son) persistently pursued their litigation rights. The plaintiff's standing as a right holder was consistently maintained. The defendant, as the obligor, had a clear historical trajectory and succession of rights and obligations. From Daido Kaiun Kaisha, Ltd. at the time of the contract, to its merger into Nippon Yusen Kaisha in 1964, then to the merger of Nippon Yusen Kaisha into Navix Line in 1989, and finally to the merger of Navix Line into Mitsui O.S.K. in 1999. Despite the changing times, the identity of the right holder and obligor between the original parties to the charterparties remained clear, and the legal succession of rights and obligations still existed. Third, the issue of limitation of action. Although the dispute arose in the 1930s, where civil rights were infringed for more than twenty years before the implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC, after its implementation, the limitation period for the right holder to seek protection from a people's court shall be calculated from January 1, 1987. According to this clear legal provision, the plaintiffs filed the lawsuit on December 30, 1988, which was within the statutory limitation period.

The effective judgment in this case was ultimately enforced through the compulsory measure of ship arrest by the court. Given that Mitsui O.S.K. failed to perform the compensation obligations determined in the effective judgment, the court, upon application by the enforcement applicant, took the compulsory measure of arresting the debtor's vessel. This fully complies with the provisions of the Special Maritime Procedure Law of the PRC and the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC.

Case 2

Maersk (China) Shipping Co., Ltd., Maersk (China) Shipping Co., Ltd. Xiamen Branch, China Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency Co., Ltd. v. Xiamen Yinghai Industrial Development Co., Ltd. — dispute over compensation for damages from infringement of international freight forwarding management rights

I. Basic Facts

Maersk (China) Shipping Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Maersk) operated international container liner services at the port of Xiamen. China Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Xiamen Ocean Agency) acted as the agent for Maersk's container shipping business. Prior to March 3, 2005, Xiamen Yinghai Industrial Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yinghai) was able to normally collect Maersk's containers from Xiamen Ocean Agency and engage in land transport businesses such as import and export container haulage. On March 3, 2005, Maersk notified Xiamen Ocean Agency to stop providing Yinghai with Maersk's containers and container seals. Yinghai then filed a lawsuit with the Xiamen Maritime Court against Maersk and others, claiming that Maersk and others refused to accept its booking for cargo on behalf of cargo owners, causing losses. Yinghai requested the court to order Maersk and others to provide freight booking and related services to Yinghai and not to refuse Yinghai from accepting mandates to handle import and export cargo shipping and land container transport business related to Maersk and others.

II. Judgment

The Xiamen Maritime Court held in the first instance that international liner companies are not common carriers and are not subject to a statutory duty to contract. Accordingly, the court dismissed Yinghai's claims. The Fujian High People's Court held in the second instance that Maersk was a common carrier and its clear statement that it would not engage in business relations with Yinghai violated the common carrier's compulsory duty to contract. The High Court therefore ruled: setting aside the first-instance judgment; ordering Maersk and others not to refuse Yinghai's booking and related transportation services in accordance with business practice. Maersk and its Xiamen Branch, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court held in the retrial that public transport refers to transport that provides public utility services and has a monopoly position. International maritime container liner services are commercial business activities serving international trade. They do not fall within public utilities, lack public welfare nature, and do not possess the characteristics of monopoly and strict price control. Therefore, they do not constitute public transport as defined in Article 289 of the Contract Law of the PRC (hereinafter referred to as the Contract Law), and the carrier is not subject to a compulsory duty to contract. On June 28, 2011, the Supreme People's Court rendered judgment: setting aside the second-instance judgment; affirming the first-instance judgment.

III. Significance

The focus of the dispute in this case was whether international liner shipping constitutes "public transport" under Article 289 of the Contract Law. The Supreme People's Court's retrial judgment in this case provides guidance and reference value at three levels. First, it filled a legislative gap. It provided a specific interpretation of "public transport" under Article 289 of the Contract Law, clarified the basic characteristics of public transport, and emphasized that the purpose of the Contract Law's provision on the compulsory duty to contract for public transport carriers is to overcome their monopoly issues. Second, it clarified a long-standing misconception in theory and practice. The retrial judgment further clarified that a liner carrier is a "common carrier" under Anglo-American law or Chinese maritime law theory, but not a "carrier engaged in public transport" under Article 289 of the Contract Law. Third, it effectively regulated the international shipping market. The international shipping industry is an important pillar industry in China. China's total container throughput at ports has ranked first in the world for many years, and ten Chinese ports are among the top twenty global container ports. The Supreme People's Court's retrial judgment established a rule of general significance for competition and development in the international shipping market, which has important practical significance.

Case 3

JPMorgan Chase Bank v. Hailiu Shipping Company — dispute over ship mortgage

I. Basic Facts

On June 19, 1997, JPMorgan Chase Bank (hereinafter referred to as JPMorgan) entered into a loan agreement with five borrowers, including Hailiu Shipping Company (hereinafter referred to as Hailiu), whereby JPMorgan agreed to provide a loan of USD 35,000,000 to the five borrowers. On June 27, 1997, JPMorgan and Hailiu entered into a deed of security, agreeing to mortgage Hailiu's vessel "Navigator" to JPMorgan to create a first priority mortgage for the USD 35,000,000 loan, and the mortgage was registered with the Registrar of Bahamian Ships in London. On July 7, 1999, JPMorgan entered into an overdraft loan agreement for USD 2,000,000 with Maritime International Co., Ltd., and Hailiu agreed to assume joint and several liability for this overdraft loan. On July 18, 2000, the parties entered into a second deed of security, again mortgaging the "Navigator" for the USD 2,000,000 overdraft loan and registering the mortgage. On March 14, 2002, JPMorgan applied to the Guangzhou Maritime Court to arrest the "Navigator" on the grounds that Hailiu had defaulted on mortgage principal and interest totaling USD 7,323,377.26. On March 15, the court ordered the arrest of the vessel. On March 22, JPMorgan filed a lawsuit with the Guangzhou Maritime Court. Subsequently, upon JPMorgan's application, the "Navigator" was lawfully auctioned, and JPMorgan purchased it for USD 5,940,000.

II. Judgment

The Guangzhou Maritime Court held after trial that the loan agreements and security deeds involved in this case were all true expressions of the parties' intent, did not violate the public interest or mandatory provisions of the PRC, and were lawful and valid. The flag state of the mortgaged vessel was the Bahamas. Pursuant to Article 271 of the Maritime Code of the PRC, the law of the flag state, i.e., the Bahamas Merchant Shipping Act, should govern the dispute over the ship mortgage. The two ship mortgages on the "Navigator" did not violate the provisions of the Bahamas Merchant Shipping Act concerning ship mortgages, and both mortgages were valid. On July 25, 2002, the Guangzhou Maritime Court rendered judgment ordering Hailiu to repay JPMorgan the loan, overdraft, interest, and related expenses. JPMorgan, based on this creditor's right, had a ship mortgage over the "Navigator" prior to its auction by the Guangzhou Maritime Court, and after the auction, was entitled to priority compensation from the auction proceeds.

III. Significance

This case is a typical dispute over a foreign-related ship mortgage. The vessel "Navigator" involved was a large oil tanker. Both the plaintiff and the defendant were foreign parties, and the facts of the case occurred abroad. However, the plaintiff JPMorgan voluntarily chose to arrest the vessel and initiate litigation in China. The maritime court applied the Bahamas Merchant Shipping Act to render its judgment, which was widely praised by the media and the international shipping community. This judgment provides strong guidance on the ascertainment and application of foreign law and the application of law in foreign-related civil relations. (A) Guidance on ascertaining foreign law. Judges should play an active guiding role in the process of ascertaining foreign law. Where parties face significant difficulties in ascertaining foreign law, judges should actively leverage their own advantages and use various lawful means to ascertain foreign law. Where it is necessary for the parties to ascertain foreign law, they should be required to provide relevant explanations and application materials for that foreign law. The ascertainment of foreign law must go through notarization and authentication procedures and be subject to cross-examination and verification in court. (B) Guidance on applying foreign law. Clarifying the nature of the legal relationship involved in the case is a prerequisite for correctly applying foreign law. In this case, with respect to the two legal relationships of the loan contract and the mortgage security, the court carefully reviewed the content of foreign law, balanced the two values of protecting domestic public interests and respecting party autonomy, and adopted a method of applying different laws to different relationships, providing important reference for future trials of similar cases. (C) Guidance on adjudicating foreign-related civil and commercial cases. The three-step adjudication approach followed in this case — "foreign-related element, jurisdiction, application of law" — has become the basic adjudication method for foreign-related civil and commercial trials in China and has broad guiding significance for the trial and adjudication of similar foreign-related civil and commercial cases.

Case 4

Zhejiang Textiles Import and Export Group Co., Ltd. v. Evergreen International Storage and Transport Co., Ltd. — dispute over contract of carriage of goods by sea

I. Basic Facts

On July 31 and August 7, 2000, Zhejiang Textiles Import and Export Group Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhejiang Textiles), as the seller, entered into a sales confirmation for school uniforms with a third party. Zhejiang Textiles, through successive agency of Huahai International Freight Co., Ltd., Honghai International Shipping and Freight Company, Shanghai Wailianfa International Freight Co., Ltd., and Shanghai Samsung International Freight Co., Ltd., booked space and shipped the goods in batches with the carrier Evergreen International Storage and Transport Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Evergreen), and obtained 21 sets of original bills of lading issued by Evergreen's agent. The shippers named in the 21 sets of bills of lading were three foreign companies. Zhejiang Textiles paid the ocean freight as required, and Evergreen confirmed receipt. After shipment, Zhejiang Textiles collected payment through bank documentary collection. No one took up the documents, and the full set of trade documents, including the bills of lading, were returned by the bank. Evergreen confirmed that it had delivered the goods to the consignee without surrender of the original bills of lading. For this reason, Zhejiang Textiles filed a lawsuit with the Shanghai Maritime Court against Evergreen, claiming compensation for the loss of the goods and other losses on the ground that Evergreen delivered the goods without presentation of original bills of lading.

II. Judgment

The Shanghai Maritime Court held after trial that Zhejiang Textiles, through successive freight forwarding agencies, booked space with the carrier Evergreen, paid freight, and delivered the goods for shipment; Evergreen accepted the goods, collected freight, and issued bills of lading as requested by Zhejiang Textiles. Although Zhejiang Textiles, in accordance with the terms of the trade contract, did not have its name stated on the bills of lading, the facts of the performance of the contract of carriage of goods by sea between Zhejiang Textiles and Evergreen proved that Zhejiang Textiles was the party that entered into the contract of carriage of goods by sea and the sole party that delivered the goods. Zhejiang Textiles' status as the shipper of the goods concerned should be recognized. Evergreen's argument that Zhejiang Textiles had transferred title to the goods solely on the basis of the shipper named in the bills of lading lacked sufficient factual and legal basis. Zhejiang Textiles was the first lawful holder of the bills of lading after their issuance; the bills of lading had not been transferred through trade channels and were returned by the bank. Its possession of the bills was lawful, and it was entitled to exercise rights under the bills of lading against the counterparty. In summary, Zhejiang Textiles had standing as the shipper of the goods involved and was entitled to assert rights under the bills of lading against Evergreen. As the carrier, Evergreen should bear liability for compensation to the shipper Zhejiang Textiles for delivery of goods without presentation of original bills of lading. The first-instance judgment ordered Evergreen to compensate Zhejiang Textiles for loss of goods of USD 2,602,562 and interest, and loss of tax refund of RMB 3,111,486.35 and interest. On September 4, 2003, the Shanghai High People's Court rendered a second-instance judgment, dismissing Evergreen's appeal and affirming the original judgment.

III. Significance

This case involves a dispute over delivery of goods without the original bill of lading in a maritime cargo transport contract with Taiwan-related elements. The central issue is whether a person who delivers goods but is not named as the shipper on the bill of lading has the legal standing as a shipper and the right to claim against the carrier. This has long been a problem affecting the protection of the rights and interests of FOB sellers in China's export trade and has been a point of legal divergence in China's maritime judicial practice. Through the trial of the facts of this case, the court determined that a person who actually delivers the goods to the carrier, accepts the bill of lading issued by the carrier, and performs the obligation to present documents to the bank under the trade contract, if the documents are returned by the bank due to non-payment, as the original holder of the bill of lading, even if not named as the shipper on the bill of lading and without endorsement under the bill, still has the legal standing as a shipper. The establishment of this principle unified different understandings of the law in judicial practice and lawfully protected the interests and transaction security of FOB sellers prevalent in China's export trade. The Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Cases of Delivery of Goods Without Original Bills of Lading, promulgated in 2009, expressly stipulated this principle in the form of judicial interpretation. In addition, the judgment in this case is the first maritime case judgment of a mainland court that has been recognized by rulings of three levels of courts in the Taiwan region, which also has positive significance for the judicial practice of mutual recognition and enforcement of civil and commercial judgments between the two sides of the Taiwan Strait.

**Case 5 Panama Yifa Shipping Company and Hong Kong Weilin Shipping Co., Ltd. v. Zhong Xiaoyuan and the Office of the Zhuhai Municipal Government for Combating Smuggling — dispute over vessel collision damage compensation**

**I. Basic Facts**

At approximately 0300 hours on November 25, 1992, the fishing vessel "Shanwei 12138", owned by Zhong Xiaoyuan and requisitioned by the Office of the Zhuhai Municipal Government for Combating Smuggling (hereinafter "Zhuhai Anti-Smuggling Office") for maritime anti-smuggling duties, was sunk after a collision. All 21 persons on board fell into the water. The colliding vessel did not rescue the persons in the water and continued sailing eastward. Of those who fell into the water, 15 were rescued, 5 others died, and 1 was declared dead. Consequently, Zhong Xiaoyuan and the Zhuhai Anti-Smuggling Office filed a lawsuit with the Guangzhou Maritime Court, alleging that the vessel "Yifa", owned by Panama Yifa Shipping Company (hereinafter "Yifa Company"), was the vessel that collided with and sank "Shanwei 12138", and requested an order for Yifa Company to compensate for all losses.

**II. Judgment**

The Guangzhou Maritime Court held at first instance that the "Yifa" vessel collided with "Shanwei 12138", causing the latter to sink, and should bear full liability for the personal injuries and property losses caused by the collision. The first instance judgment ordered Yifa Company to pay Zhong Xiaoyuan RMB 2,390,400 and HKD 20,000, plus interest on both amounts; and to pay the Zhuhai Anti-Smuggling Office RMB 226,420 and HKD 34,276, plus interest on both amounts. The Guangdong High People's Court, in the second instance, dismissed Yifa Company's appeal and affirmed the original judgment. Yifa Company and Hong Kong Weilin Shipping Co., Ltd. applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court, in the retrial, held that Zhong Xiaoyuan and the Zhuhai Anti-Smuggling Office, as the parties claiming that the "Yifa" vessel was the colliding vessel that sank "Shanwei 12138", should bear the corresponding burden of proof. Due to the facts that there were no collision marks or damage on the bow of the "Yifa" vessel, the paint samples taken from the port side of the "Yifa" vessel were not identical to the paint of "Shanwei 12138", the "Yifa" vessel did not make a sharp left turn or reduce speed when passing the accident area, the relative positions of the alleged collision site and the locations where the sunken vessel and rescued persons were found were inconsistent with the prevailing currents at the time of the accident, and there was objective evidence that a container vessel which had departed from Hong Kong passed through the accident area sailing eastward at the time of the collision, the evidence was insufficient to establish that the "Yifa" vessel was the colliding vessel. The Supreme People's Court rendered a judgment on May 18, 1999, reversing the first and second instance judgments in this case and dismissing the claims of Zhong Xiaoyuan and the Zhuhai Anti-Smuggling Office.

**III. Typical Significance**

This case is the first vessel collision dispute case publicly tried by the Supreme People's Court. In maritime adjudication, the lack of direct evidence to establish the collision facts is a difficulty in hearing disputes over vessel collision damage compensation. All evidence pointing to the "Yifa" vessel as the colliding vessel in this case was circumstantial evidence. In response, the retrial judgment in this case, applying the rules of evidence, using logical reasoning and the rules of experience, and combining the civil litigation standard of proof of "high probability", comprehensively evaluated all evidence and established the basic principle that circumstantial evidence can only establish the existence of collision facts when it mutually corroborates and forms a complete chain of evidence. This principle has guiding significance for judicial practice on how to use circumstantial evidence to determine the facts of a collision. The retrial hearing process in this case was also noteworthy. To ensure the objectivity of expert evaluations, the technical appraisal report was read out in court by the expert, and the parties cross-examined it in court. The use of this cross-examination procedure played a positive and decisive role in ultimately obtaining a fair judgment in this case. Furthermore, during the retrial of this case, evidentiary documents that had been confirmed by courts in the Taiwan region were admitted, which at the time had reference value for resolving the issue of evidence acceptance between courts in Mainland China and the Taiwan region.

**Case 6 Hainan Fenghai Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Industry Co., Ltd. v. The People's Insurance (Property) Company of China, Ltd., Hainan Provincial Branch — dispute over marine cargo insurance contract**

**I. Basic Facts**

On November 28, 1995, Hainan Fenghai Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Industry Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Fenghai Company") insured 4,999.85 metric tons of palm oil in drums carried by the vessel "HAGAAG" with The People's Insurance (Property) Company of China, Ltd., Hainan Provincial Branch (hereinafter "PICC Hainan"). The insurance coverage was "All Risks". According to the insurance clauses, the coverage of All Risks includes, in addition to the liabilities under FPA (Free from Particular Average) and WPA (With Particular Average) coverage, "all loss of or damage to the insured goods from any external cause during the course of transit." The clauses also specified five exclusions. After the "HAGAAG" vessel set sail from November 23 to 29, 1995, due to a dispute over charter hire between the shipowner and the time charterer, the "HAGAAG" abandoned the voyage stipulated in the bill of lading and blocked external information about the vessel's movements, until April 1996 when the "HAGAAG" was caught smuggling into Shanwei, China by Chinese maritime police. According to the Determination of Exemption from Prosecution (No. Suijianxing Jianmian Zi (1996) 64) issued by the Guangzhou People's Procuratorate, the palm oil carried on the "HAGAAG" had either been stolen and sold, or was confiscated and turned over to the state treasury by the Chinese procuratorial authorities as smuggled goods. Fenghai Company filed a claim with PICC Hainan, which explicitly refused to pay. Fenghai Company then filed a lawsuit with the Haikou Maritime Court.

**II. Judgment**

The Haikou Maritime Court held at first instance that the loss of the insured goods in this case was caused by the shipowner's acts of stealing, selling, and smuggling, which were external causes unforeseeable and uncontrollable by Fenghai Company, and therefore fell within the coverage of the All Risks insurance procured by Fenghai Company. The first instance judgment ordered PICC Hainan to compensate Fenghai Company for the insured value loss of USD 3,593,858.75. The Hainan High People's Court, in the second instance, held that according to the insurance clauses attached to the insurance policy and industry practice, the scope of liability under All Risks is classified as "specified risks", including FPA, WPA, and ordinary additional risks. The loss of the insured goods of Fenghai Company did not fall within the scope of liability under All Risks. The second instance judgment reversed the first instance judgment and dismissed Fenghai Company's claims. Fenghai Company applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court, in the retrial, held that the loss of the subject matter insured in this case did not fall within the exclusions specified in the insurance clauses, and was caused by external factors beyond the control of the consignee (the insured, Fenghai Company). The insured event in this case fell within the scope of liability under All Risks. The Supreme People's Court rendered a judgment on July 13, 2004, reversing the second instance judgment of the Hainan High People's Court and affirming the first instance judgment of the Haikou Maritime Court.

**III. Typical Significance**

The central issue in this case was how to interpret the scope of liability under All Risks in the marine cargo insurance clauses. This issue has consistently been subject to differing views in maritime insurance law theory and judicial practice. The courts of first and second instance in this case rendered diametrically opposite judgments. The Supreme People's Court's judgment in this case provided a definitive conclusion on the interpretation of All Risks under the marine cargo insurance clauses. The All Risks coverage under the relevant "Marine Cargo Insurance Clauses" includes, in addition to liabilities under FPA and WPA, all loss of or damage to the insured goods from any external cause during the course of transit. In the absence of intentional misconduct or negligence by the insured, unless the loss of the insured goods falls within the exclusions under the insurance contract, the insurer shall bear all losses arising from external causes during the course of transit. Through its reversal of the judgment in this case, the Supreme People's Court established the following principles: 1. All Risks is not a "specified risk" but rather a "non-specified risk." 2. The loss of the subject matter insured must be caused by an external cause. 3. The external cause must be limited to occurrences during the course of transit. This judgment's determination of the scope of All Risks has important guiding significance for the unification of subsequent judicial practice.

**Case 7 He Yuantang, Xu Ji'anben, He Yuanjiu v. Guangxi Hepu Xichang Yongxin Sugar Co., Ltd. — dispute over compensation for marine fisheries pollution damage**

**I. Basic Facts**

The clam farm jointly operated by He Yuantang and others, covering 312 mu, was located in the high sand sea area at the mouth of the Hougang River, Xichang Town, Hepu County. The national sea area use permit they had obtained had expired, and they had no aquaculture permit. In October 2003, Guangxi Hepu Xichang Yongxin Sugar Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Yongxin Sugar Company") began sugar production. In mid-November 2003, a large number of clams belonging to He Yuantang and others died. On November 25, the Beihai Environmental Monitoring Center's monitoring results showed that the wastewater discharged from the 35-ton boiler ash flushing water outlet of Yongxin Sugar Company severely exceeded standards. On January 8, 2004, the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region Fisheries Environmental Monitoring Center issued the "Expert Appraisal Report on Fisheries Pollution Accident Investigation," which concluded that based on the test results of the Aquatic Biotechnology Laboratory of the Guangxi Fisheries Research Institute, the possibility of the clams dying from disease was essentially ruled out; the COD (Chemical Oxygen Demand) at the clam farm site was as high as 11.4 mg/L, indicating that the sea area had been polluted by foreign pollutants. On March 30, nine experts, including Li Qinan, Senior Engineer of the Fisheries Administration Division of the Guangxi Aquatic Products and Animal Husbandry Bureau, issued the "Expert Opinion on the Assessment of Losses of Clam Farms Polluted in Xichang Town, Hepu County," assessing the loss of clams due to pollution at 2,118,000 kilograms. On May 10, the Fisheries Administration Division of the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region Aquatic Products Bureau issued the "Conclusion on the Pollution Incident Affecting Cultured Clams in Xichang Town, Hepu County, Guangxi": The cause of death of the clams at the Xichang Town, Hepu County clam farms in November 2003 was wastewater discharged by Yongxin Sugar Company that severely exceeded the national discharge standards, resulting in the loss of 2,118,000 kilograms of clams, with direct economic losses of no less than RMB 9,319,200. Based on this, He Yuantang and others filed a lawsuit with the Beihai Maritime Court.

**II. Judgment**

The Beihai Maritime Court held at first instance that there was a necessary causal relationship between the damage to the clams farmed by He Yuantang and others and Yongxin Sugar Company's discharge of pollutants exceeding standards, and Yongxin Sugar Company should bear liability for compensation for the losses. The aquaculture activities of He Yuantang and others were illegal; therefore, the income loss from farming the clams was not protected. However, the property loss from purchasing clam seedlings should be appropriately protected. Because He Yuantang and others had arbitrarily placed clam seedlings for farming, their conduct was negligent, and they should bear primary responsibility, assuming 60% of the liability for the loss of clam seedlings, while Yongxin Sugar Company assumed 40% liability. The first instance judgment ordered Yongxin Sugar Company to pay He Yuantang and others RMB 300,484 for the loss of clam seedlings and dismissed the other claims. The Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region High People's Court rendered a judgment on December 20, 2005, dismissing Yongxin Sugar Company's appeal and affirming the original judgment.

**III. Typical Significance**

This case is a dispute over compensation for aquaculture damage caused by land-based pollution accepted by a maritime court. Its typical significance lies in clarifying the basic principle that income from aquaculture obtained without an aquaculture permit and a sea area use right certificate cannot be protected by law. The basis of a tort claim is that the tortfeasor's wrongful act infringes upon legally protected legitimate interests. Only under this premise does the tortfeasor bear liability for the damage caused by the tortious act. In this case, He Yuantang and others had neither a sea area use certificate nor an aquaculture permit; their aquaculture activities were illegal, and the income generated from such farming should not be protected by law. However, He Yuantang and others had legitimate property rights and interests in the clam seedlings they purchased with raised funds. These legitimate rights and interests should not be forfeited simply because of the illegality of their farming activities and should be afforded a certain degree of legal protection. The establishment of this principle reflects both the legal consequences of unlicensed aquaculture and the legal liability for unlawful infringement of others' property rights, fully embodying the legal objective of encouraging the lawful use of marine resources for development while also vigorously strengthening environmental protection and resource management.

**Case 8 Qian'an No. 1 Paper Mill and Eight Other Enterprises v. Sun Youli and Eighteen Others — dispute over aquaculture damage compensation**

**I. Basic Facts**

In 1997, Sun Youli and eighteen others signed a partnership agreement to raise capital and jointly establish six seafood farms. The legal farming qualifications of the six farms were approved and confirmed by relevant authorities. In early and mid-October 2000, a major fisheries pollution accident occurred in the aquaculture areas of the Luanhe River and Daqing River estuaries in Wangtan Town, Leting County, causing substantial economic losses to the farming areas of Sun Youli and the others. Sun Youli and the others filed a lawsuit against Qian'an No. 1 Paper Mill and eight other enterprises with the Tianjin Maritime Court. Upon entrustment by the first instance court for appraisal, it was determined that this pollution accident was caused by the nine enterprises, including Qian'an No. 1 Paper Mill, directly discharging large amounts of wastewater into the Luanhe River, which then entered the sea through various coastal drainage sluices in Leting County, causing severe organic and suspended solids pollution in the nearshore farming sea area. It was also found that among the nine enterprises, Hebei Qian'an Chemical Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Chemical Company") was discharging in compliance with standards.

**II. Judgment**

The Tianjin Maritime Court held at first instance that there was a causal relationship between the pollutant discharge of the nine enterprises and the damage suffered by Sun Youli and the others. Although the Chemical Company was discharging in compliance with standards, it could not sufficiently prove that there was no causal relationship between its wastewater discharge and the damage to Sun Youli and the others, and therefore should bear liability for compensation. The court rendered a judgment ordering the nine enterprises, including Qian'an No. 1 Paper Mill, to jointly and severally compensate Sun Youli and the others for economic losses of RMB 13,659,700. The Tianjin High People's Court, in the second instance, held that the Chemical Company had been confirmed by the local environmental protection authority as an enterprise discharging within standards, which was a normal business activity permitted by the state. Although the Chemical Company could not provide evidence showing that there was no causal relationship between its discharge of industrial wastewater into the sea and the farming losses of Sun Youli and the others, its civil liability should be distinguished from that of enterprises that exceeded standards. The Tianjin High People's Court rendered a judgment on March 24, 2003, modifying the first instance judgment, ordering the Chemical Company to bear RMB 140,000 in damages independently, and the other eight enterprises, including Qian'an No. 1 Paper Mill, to bear RMB 6,553,250 in damages jointly and severally.

**III. Typical Significance**

This case is a landmark judicial decision by the People's Court clarifying that in land-based pollution cases, even if the discharge meets standards, the polluter should still bear appropriate liability for environmental pollution damage compensation. This effectively punished land-based pollution generators, effectively protected the marine environment of the Bohai Rim region, and marked a further integration of China's environmental protection work with advanced international standards. It is an important milestone in the rule of law process of China's environmental protection and has served as a reference for subsequent judicial practice in environmental pollution cases and even the formulation of relevant provisions in the Tort Liability Law. In adjudicating such cases, courts must, on one hand, fulfill the important function of adjudication to punish polluters and protect the rights of victims; on the other hand, based on the principle of fairness, they should scientifically and reasonably apportion liability among tortfeasors according to whether their discharge exceeded standards. During the trial of this case, the laws and regulations concerning joint torts and environmental pollution were incomplete. The court's discretionary decision to order the Chemical Company to bear independent civil liability rather than joint and several liability fully embodied the principle of consistency between fault and liability, was conducive to encouraging enterprises to meet discharge standards, upheld the fairness of the law, and achieved good results under the specific historical conditions at that time.

**Case 9 Application by China Shipping Development Co., Ltd. Freight Company for the Establishment of a Fund for Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims**

**I. Basic Facts**

The vessel "Ning An 11", owned by China Shipping Development Co., Ltd. Freight Company (hereinafter "Freight Company"), was transporting thermal coal from Qinhuangdao to the Waigaoqiao Terminal in Shanghai on May 23, 2008. On May 26, while berthing, it collided with the No. 2 ship unloader at the terminal, causing damage to the terminal and machinery. On March 9, 2009, Freight Company, pursuant to Article 210(2) of the Maritime Code of the PRC (hereinafter "Maritime Code") and Article 4 of the Provisions of the Ministry of Communications on the Limits of Maritime Claims for Vessels of Less Than 300 Gross Tonnage and Vessels Engaged in Coastal Transport or Coastal Operations, applied to the Shanghai Maritime Court for the establishment of a limitation fund for non-personal injury maritime claims. The Shanghai Branch of The People's Insurance Company (Property) of China Ltd. (hereinafter "PICC Shanghai Branch") and others raised objections, arguing: Freight Company was fully liable for the accident and was not entitled to limit its liability; the costs for clearing the wreck involved in the accident constituted non-limitable claims; and the vessel "Ning An 11" was a vessel capable of engaging in international ocean-going transport and did not fall within the category of vessels engaged in cargo transport between Chinese ports, and thus should be subject to the limitation amount specified in Article 210(1)(2) of the Maritime Code.

**II. Judgment**

The Shanghai Maritime Court held at first instance that the objection by PICC Shanghai Branch and others that Freight Company was not entitled to limitation of liability involved a determination of whether Freight Company had the substantive right to limit its liability, which should be resolved in the substantive trial of the case. Therefore, the court did not address this objection in the fund establishment proceeding. The objection that the wreck clearance costs constituted non-limitable claims did not affect the court's decision to grant Freight Company's application for the establishment of a limitation fund for maritime claims relating to the limitable claims involved. The business transport certificate of the vessel "Ning An 11" specified its approved scope of operation as "transport of ordinary goods between ports along the domestic coast and in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River." At the time of the accident, it was precisely engaged in a voyage from Qinhuangdao Port to Shanghai Port. Therefore, this vessel should be regarded as a "vessel engaged in transport between ports of the PRC," and the determination should not be based on the navigable areas indicated on the vessel's seaworthiness certificate or the areas the vessel is capable of navigating. Freight Company's calculation of the amount of the limitation fund in this case was not improper. The first instance court granted the application for Freight Company to establish a limitation fund for maritime claims. The Shanghai High People's Court rendered an order on July 27, 2009, dismissing PICC Shanghai Branch's appeal and affirming the first instance order.

**III. Typical Significance**

The focal point of this case lies in the scope of review for applications to establish a fund for limitation of liability for maritime claims and the definition of ships engaged in transport between Chinese ports. For a long time, there has been theoretical controversy regarding the scope of review for such applications. In judicial practice, there have also been different understandings of the phrase "ships engaged in transport between the ports of the People's Republic of China" as stipulated in Article 210, paragraph 2 of the Maritime Code. This case clarifies that the court's review of an application to establish a fund for limitation of liability for maritime claims should be limited to a procedural review of three aspects: the applicant's eligibility, the nature of the claims involved in the accident, and the amount of the fund applied for. This is conducive to ensuring the efficiency and effectiveness of trials in such cases. This case establishes that "ships engaged in transport between the ports of the People's Republic of China" should be understood as ships that, on the voyage in which the maritime accident occurred, were engaged in transport between Chinese ports. This provides demonstrative guidance for the adjudication of similar cases and is of significant importance for protecting the legitimate rights and interests of China's domestic coastal transport industry.

Case 10: First Investment Company of the Marshall Islands v. Fujian Mawei Shipbuilding Co., Ltd. and Fujian Shipbuilding Industry Group Co., Ltd. — application for recognition and enforcement of an arbitral award rendered by a London ad hoc arbitral tribunal

I. Basic Facts

On September 15, 2003, the respondent Fujian Mawei Shipbuilding Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Mawei Company) and the respondent Fujian Shipbuilding Industry Group Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Fujian Shipbuilding Group), as joint sellers, signed an Option Agreement with First Investment Company (hereinafter FIC), registered in the Republic of the Marshall Islands and belonging to the Greek Restis Group, concerning the construction of vessels. The agreement stipulated that the two respondents irrevocably agreed to enter into Option Vessel Construction Contracts with FIC or its designee for a maximum of eight vessels. Any dispute arising out of or in connection with the agreement was to be submitted to arbitration in London; the arbitration proceedings, including the enforcement of the arbitral award, were to be governed by the Arbitration Act 1996 (UK) or any then-current amendment or re-enactment thereof and the then-current rules of the London Maritime Arbitrators Association (hereinafter LMAA Rules); each party was to appoint one arbitrator, and the two arbitrators so appointed were to select the third arbitrator. Thereafter, within the declaration period stipulated in the Option Agreement, FIC declared eight option vessels effective, demanding that the respondents enter into Option Vessel Construction Contracts for eight vessels with eight single-ship companies designated by FIC, and sent the contract texts it provided for signature, but the two respondents did not sign within the period. On June 4, 2004, FIC and the eight designated companies initiated arbitration in London, England, requesting that the two respondents be jointly and severally liable for their commercial losses of USD 45.4 million plus interest, and appointed Mr. Harris as arbitrator. The respondents appointed Mr. Wang Shengchang as arbitrator. Mr. Harris and Mr. Wang Shengchang jointly appointed Mr. Martin Hunter as the third arbitrator. After two hearings, on January 21, 2006, the presiding arbitrator, Mr. Martin Hunter, produced the first draft of the arbitral award in the case and distributed it to Mr. Wang Shengchang and Mr. Harris for review. On February 16, 2006, Mr. Wang Shengchang submitted a draft of his dissenting opinion. On March 20, 2006, Mr. Wang Shengchang was criminally detained by the First Branch of Tianjin Municipal People's Procuratorate on suspicion of committing a crime, and was arrested on March 31, 2006 with the approval of that procuratorate. From the time of his criminal detention, Mr. Wang Shengchang had no further contact with Mr. Martin Hunter and Mr. Harris. He did not see the second draft of the award sent to him by Mr. Martin Hunter on March 25, 2006, or the final version of March 31. His participation in the case ended with the "draft opinion" he had issued on the first draft of the award. Pursuant to Article 8(e) of the LMAA Rules, which provides that "after the appointment of the third arbitrator, decisions, orders and arbitral awards shall be made by all or a majority of the arbitrators," Mr. Martin Hunter and Mr. Harris dated and published the arbitral award on June 19, 2006, as a majority decision of the arbitral tribunal, awarding the respondents to pay FIC compensation of USD 26.4 million plus interest and compound interest on that amount. On December 5, 2006, FIC filed an application with the Xiamen Maritime Court, requesting recognition of the arbitral award as legally effective within the territory of the People's Republic of China and its enforcement, in accordance with the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards (hereinafter the New York Convention).

II. Judgment

The Xiamen Maritime Court held that the application of Article 8(e) of the LMAA Rules to an arbitration case presupposes that every arbitrator in the arbitral tribunal participated in the entire arbitration proceedings; otherwise, the majority of the arbitrators are not authorized to make an arbitral award. On this basis, the court determined that the arbitration proceedings of the arbitral tribunal did not conform to the arbitration agreement agreed upon by the parties, nor did they conform to the law of the place of arbitration, the United Kingdom. Pursuant to Article 267 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 5(1)(d) of the New York Convention, the Xiamen Maritime Court ruled on May 11, 2008 that the arbitral award would not be recognized and enforced.

III. Significance

This case, in which a Chinese court refused to recognize and enforce an arbitral award rendered by a truncated tribunal, has had a certain impact in the international arbitration community. The focal point of this case is how to determine the validity of a truncated arbitral award when, in the later stages of the arbitration proceedings, one arbitrator becomes unable to continue performing his duties, and the remaining members of the arbitral tribunal proceed with the arbitration and render an award. In this case, the arbitration agreement explicitly provided that the arbitral tribunal was to consist of three arbitrators. Neither the Arbitration Act 1996 (UK) nor the LMAA Rules contain provisions for truncated tribunal proceedings. Nevertheless, the arbitral tribunal, in circumstances where one arbitrator did not participate in the entire arbitration proceedings, applied Article 8(e) of the LMAA Rules concerning majority decisions to render an award. This constituted a situation where the arbitration proceedings of the arbitral tribunal did not conform to the arbitration agreement agreed upon by the parties, as provided for in the New York Convention. The court therefore ruled to refuse recognition and enforcement of the arbitral award. The New York Convention, hailed as the cornerstone of international commercial arbitration, sets international standards for the recognition and enforcement of foreign arbitral awards and is recognized by most countries. As of the end of March 2014, the Convention had 149 contracting states. As a contracting state, China's system for the recognition and enforcement of foreign arbitral awards has essentially aligned with internationally prevailing practices. In this case, the Chinese court accurately grasped the purpose and spirit of the Convention, correctly interpreted and applied its provisions, and equally protected the legitimate rights of both Chinese and foreign parties.
